articles.title: Prince and Princess of Wales in India ahead of meeting with Modi
articles.summary: Most of the engagements the royal couple will attend are related to the Earthshot Prize, which Prince William founded.
articles.body:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years.

Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week.

Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five £1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges.

"The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals.

"She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come."

The meeting with Modi was a late addition to the royal schedule after the Indian prime minister confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.

They will fly from Mumbai to Delhi for the meeting on Wednesday.

"For the Prince, it represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage," a Kensington Palace spokesperson said.

"We've seen him increasingly support the UK's diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level."

The couple last met Modi on their official visit to India in 2016.

Arriving in Mumbai earlier on Monday Prince William posted a message about the trip on social media: "India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country."

The royals will carry out a number of engagements in Mumbai related to the environment, cricket, young families and the Bollywood film industry.

At an Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony, five innovations will be announced as winners of the million-pound prizes.

Nominees range from projects to increase the number of electric rickshaws in India to a scheme able to detect wildfires faster than Nasa.

The event will be hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Take That will perform and guests will include actor Rami Malek and Australian conservationist and TV presenter Robert Irwin, who joined Prince William when he was a surprise guest on The Graham Norton show last month .

"There is a lot of environmental potential here in Mumbai," said Irwin. "There is also a huge amount of young people who have a passion for environmentalism and I think Earthshot is mobilising that here in India."

articles.title: Investors sue chip giant Intel after 29% stock plunge
articles.summary: A proposed class action says Intel hid the impact of slowing sales, inflating its shares.
articles.body:
Shareholders have sued US chip giant Intel, accusing it of hiding the severity of a slump in personal computer (PC) sales, which they say led to a nearly 29% one-day collapse in the firm's stock.

A proposed class action lawsuit in San Jose, California said Intel was too late to alert shareholders about how slowing sales could impact its earnings, allegedly artificially inflating its stock price.

Intel shares plunged on 30 October, erasing tens of billions of dollars off its market value the day after it forecasted disappointing revenue in its coming earnings report.

The BBC has contacted Intel for comment.

The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders.

Intel has been accused of making "materially false and/or misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, the complaint said.

In October, the firm announced that its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from Intel that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit said the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings – a drop of 9%, or about $800m, to $8.1bn.

Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power.

As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive.

Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs.

"We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October.

Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though the stock is still up by 51% overall this year.

articles.title: Indonesian president apologises to Singapore, Malaysia for wildfire haze
articles.summary: Prabowo says his government has a ‘zero-tolerance policy’ for firms that contribute to blazes and pledges strict action.
articles.body:
⁠Indonesian President ⁠Prabowo Subianto has apologised to Singapore and Malaysia ⁠for the transboundary haze due to months-long wildfires.

Prabowo conveyed the apology during a session at the ASEAN summit that kicked off on Sunday in the Philippine capital, Manila, according to a statement from the Indonesian presidential office.

“I would like to apologise to my neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore when we had a very big forest fire, which took nearly four months for us to control. The haze travelled to Malaysia and to Singapore. It is not not our fault but once again we apologise but we have done our best,” he said.

Prabowo also said his government had and would continue to take firm ‌action on companies involved in forest fires while also preparing to establish a new body to strengthen wildfire prevention.

Indonesia has a “zero-tolerance policy” for any company contributing to the blazes, the statement quoted him as saying.

“We’ve revoked 17 concessions [permits] from companies. [Meanwhile] 26 companies are currently under investigation and 11 others have been charged. Another 23 companies are on the list to be charged,” he said.

“In total, 104 companies are currently under investigation by our police.”

He also said Indonesia had deployed 71,000 forest firefighters, and 16 people died while battling the blazes.

Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told a news briefing later on Sunday that Jakarta was “very frank and candid in expressing the efforts they have been exerting in addressing the forest fires in Indonesia” during the plenary session.

Indonesia has been battling its ‌ most intense wildfires in 11 years , with large swaths of land scorched, mainly on the islands ‌of ‌Sumatra, Borneo and Papua.

Haze from the fires blanketed some of its nearest neighbours, primarily Singapore and Malaysia, over the past few months.

Malaysia and Singapore have refrained from criticising Indonesia, instead offering assistance to fight the fires.

Previously, an Indonesian official faced criticism after claiming the country’s forests supply oxygen to Malaysia and Singapore despite recurring haze from wildfires.

“We do not just send smoke, but when there is no smoke, we send oxygen,” Indonesian Government Communications Agency chief Syahganda Nainggolan said in October.

On paper, Southeast Asian countries are committed to working together to prevent cross-border air pollution under the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

The legally binding treaty commits the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to tackle haze, a recurring issue for decades, through “concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international co-operation”.

However, the agreement does not contain provisions for enforcement by a judicial body such as the International Court of Justice. Disagreements over interpretation and application can only be settled through negotiation.

Implementation of the treaty has also moved at a snail’s pace. The treaty’s coordinating office in Jakarta only opened this April, nearly a quarter-century after it was envisioned.

Prabowo’s remarks came as the problem of transboundary haze has begun to disappear.

On Thursday, the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) issued a “no transboundary smoke haze” notice for southern parts of Southeast Asia, the Jakarta Post reported. The relief has been linked to recent downpours and fewer fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces.

articles.title: Isaac, a cat missing since Brooklyn building collapsed, is reunited with owner
articles.summary: A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday.
articles.body: A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday. Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman. It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday’s collapse, which killed eight people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives. Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah’s apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn’t been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been. Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat’s cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for a checkup. “I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Zariah told the Times. “I knew they would.” Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: “I just really hope they come and get our cat. He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah’s reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor’s office, the city’s Buildings Department and the nonprofit for the happy outcome. “Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We’re grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”

articles.title: Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025
articles.summary: Chinese tech executive romantically linked to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left in August 2025, Singapore-based firm says.
articles.body:
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, the tech executive whose reported relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of international spying claims, left the company last year.

The Singapore-based data centre company said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang left her executive role on August 30, 2025, and has held no position with the firm since.

“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” the statement said.

Megaspeed also pushed back on media reports it said contained claims about its operations that “are not supported by verifiable evidence”.

“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said.

Megaspeed, a major buyer of graphics processing units (GPUs) made by the California-based Nvidia, used to train and run frontier AI models, is facing scrutiny over its compliance with United States export controls intended to keep high-end chips out of China.

While data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand can import high-end Nvidia chips legally, US authorities have long suspected the region is a hotbed of illicit smuggling on behalf of Chinese AI developers.

Megaspeed CEO and chairman Tan Yong Pong said on Thursday that the company had retained a top US law firm to lead a “comprehensive census” of its GPUs and verify its export control compliance practices.

Unnamed US officials have accused Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security in an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia CEO , president and board member on Thursday amid a board investigation.

Beijing has denied the allegations, describing them as “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims.

Singaporean authorities are investigating Megaspeed on suspicion of making false declarations in relation to its purchases of servers. They said last week they had previously confiscated Alice Huang’s passport for eight months as part of their inquiries.

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that it barred Huang from re-entering the country after determining that she had provided inaccurate information to investigators to downplay her role at Megaspeed.

Police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing, the ministry said in a statement.

articles.title: Days after resigning over affair, Jensen Huang ‘talks’ return as Nvidia CEO; ‘Everyone loves Jensen’ call, ‘war room’ and more that could bring him back
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is weighing a return as Nvidia’s chief executive, just four days after he resigned from the company he co-founded and ran for 33 years.
articles.body: Jensen Huang is weighing a return as Nvidia’s chief executive, just four days after he resigned from the company he co-founded and ran for 33 years. The former Nvidia CEO has discussed the possibility of a comeback with close confidantes, according to a Financial Times report citing multiple people familiar with the matter. This comes even as an independent probe ordered by Nvidia’s board continues to look into the conduct that led to his exit.Huang stepped down as president, CEO and director on November 12. His resignation followed reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who has been accused of spying for China, and with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. A report of a third relationship, with another Nvidia employee, surfaced hours after he left. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and the $4 trillion chipmaker reports its quarterly results on Tuesday.Jensen Huang’s allies are building a ‘war room’ to lobby Nvidia’s boardOne Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to push for the former CEO’s return. The group will also try to win over the White House, and the effort reportedly has Huang’s backing.“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said.Two large Nvidia shareholders have also left the door open. On Friday, Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker wrote to the board urging it to keep “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang”.Even his allies aren’t sure how to repair his reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence,” one person involved in the effort acknowledged to the FT.Elon Musk and over 8,000 Nvidia employees have signed the ‘Bring Jensen Back’ letterThe public face of the campaign is an open letter urging the board to “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. By Monday morning India time, it carried 169,588 names, with 8,364 identifying themselves as current Nvidia employees. That is close to 20% of the company’s roughly 42,000-strong workforce.The numbers come with a caveat. The campaign itself says affiliations are self-reported and not verified, and reports have flagged entries such as “Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor”.The marquee names are real, though. Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator’s Garry Tan, Shopify’s Tobias Lutke and Replit CEO Amjad Masad are all on the list. Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick wrote that Huang had “erred, yes”, but added, “I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company.”Inside Nvidia, an internal suggestion box post asking the board to weigh employee sentiment has drawn more than 1,600 comments, most of them backing Huang. The campaign is also nudging institutional investors to raise the issue on Tuesday’s earnings call at 5pm ET, which is 3:30am IST on Wednesday.Silicon Valley has seen this play out before. In 2023, OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman and reinstated him within days after staff and investors revolted.Washington and Nvidia’s board structure stand in the way of Huang’s returnIn Washington, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” he said in a television interview.He also wants Nvidia to explain within 10 days whether it knowingly let its most advanced AI chips reach China. He called that more important than the affair.Huang has limited leverage inside the company as well. Unlike several other founder-CEOs, he does not hold a controlling stake and cannot overrule the board, the FT noted. The board, now chaired by former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones, has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor, though Nvidia said no “formal” process has begun.The Alice Huang angle got murkier over the weekend. Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips, said she left the company “effective Aug. 30, 2025” and currently has no role there.Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, though no date has been set. Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment to the FT.In 2023, Huang said he could run Nvidia for another three or four decades. Whether he gets that chance now rests with a board he can’t outvote and a government that wants someone new.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: A British D-Day veteran left three wartime medals on his uniform when he returned it in 1945; more than 80 years later, a young historian helped the 103-year-old obtain replacements for Remembrance Day
articles.summary: Douglas Halley, a 103-year-old British D-Day veteran, has been reunited with three wartime medals he lost in 1945 after accidentally leaving them pinned
articles.body: Douglas Halley, a 103-year-old British D-Day veteran, has been reunited with three wartime medals he lost in 1945 after accidentally leaving them pinned to the uniform he returned at the end of World War II. The medals, the 1939 to 45 Star, the France and Germany Star, and the War Medal 1939 to 45, arrived just in time for Remembrance Day, thanks to the help of a young historian and the UK Ministry of Defence, according to Good News Network and Yahoo News.Halley served in the Royal Artillery and landed on the Normandy beaches during Operation Overlord as part of the second wave of troops. More than eight decades later, he can once again wear the honours that recognise his service, an outcome his family describes as deeply meaningful. Read more about this incident, as per the reports, here:A young man called to warHalley was born in South Yorkshire, England, and was training to become a butcher when he was called up to serve in 1943. He was just 20 years old when he joined the war effort, a fact that makes his later survival and long life even more striking.His role in the Royal Artillery involved operating the Bren light machine gun, a weapon he later said was the reason he is losing his hearing. After the war, he remained in the forces until the 1950s before returning to civilian life.When he landed in Normandy in June 1944, he was part of the second wave of troops during Operation Overlord. He has described slipping from a rope ladder as he descended from his ship, falling into the water, and then running for cover as machine gun fire broke out around him.The medals he lostHalley was awarded three medals for his service: the 1939 to 45 Star, the France and Germany Star, and the War Medal 1939 to 45. These honours recognise participation in major campaigns and service during the war years.But in 1945, when he returned his uniform at the end of the war, the medals were still attached. That simple mistake meant he lost them at the very moment they had become some of the most prestigious honours he would ever receive.For 81 years, the medals remained missing. Halley carried the memory of what they represented, but he did not have the physical objects to show for it.A historian found the recordIn January 2026, 27-year-old Joseph Smith came across Halley’s military record while researching veterans’ stories for a project called The Last of the Greats. Smith, along with three friends, has been travelling across the UK documenting the experiences of surviving veterans so younger generations can learn about and remember their sacrifices.Smith saw a Facebook post from Halley’s grandson, Luke Halley, about his grandfather’s story. He contacted Luke to ask whether the family still had the medals, not knowing that they had been lost decades earlier.Once he learned what had happened, Smith did not stop there. He helped the family contact the Ministry of Defence and fill out the necessary forms to request the medals’ return.The Ministry of Defence respondedThe Ministry of Defence successfully located Halley’s medals and agreed to mail them back to him. On November 10, 2026, the medals arrived by post, more than 80 years after they were first lost.For Halley, the moment was emotional. He said he was “delighted” to have the medals back for himself and his family, and especially grateful that they arrived in time for Remembrance Day, as per the reports.He also thanked Smith for tracing the medals and ensuring they were returned safely. “They may be just a piece of metal, but the medals are something that I hold very close to my heart... They remind me of all my brothers in arms who I was with who helped me get through in the war," Halley said, reported Talker News.What the medals mean nowFor the Halley family, the returned medals are more than a personal keepsake. They are a tangible link to a chapter of history that is rapidly disappearing as the number of living World War II veterans continues to shrink.Luke Halley said the family plans to display the medals alongside photographs of his grandfather in his army uniform. He described the medals as a “lovely keepsake” that can be shared with family members and passed down through generations.That kind of preservation matters. It turns a private family memory into something that can be seen, discussed, and understood by people who never met the veteran themselves.A reminder about remembranceHalley’s story is a reminder that remembrance is not only about ceremonies and public holidays. It is also about the small, personal acts that keep history alive, whether that means recording a veteran’s story, helping a family recover a lost medal, or simply listening to someone who lived through it.Smith’s work through The Last of the Greats reflects that idea. By documenting veterans’ stories and helping families recover lost items, he is contributing to a broader effort to preserve the human side of history.For Halley, the return of his medals is a personal victory. For his family, it is a legacy. And for anyone who hears the story, it is a reminder that the sacrifices of war are not always visible, but they can still be honoured.You use AI every day. articles.title: Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote
articles.summary: Martine Moise is one of 33 registered candidates running in Haiti’s first presidential election in a decade.
articles.body:
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 ⁠assassination was ⁠a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.

Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate ⁠on Sunday.

A ⁠first-round vote is set for July next year.

Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs .

“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.

In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.

Martine Moise is one of three ‌women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.

Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.

Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led ⁠Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.

He ⁠was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.

A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of ⁠much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.

About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador .

Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.

The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.

articles.title: Beatles show keeps late Stoke-on-Trent music promoter's legacy alive
articles.summary: Mike Lloyd wrote The Rise of the Beatles as part of Stoke-on-Trent's centenary celebrations in 2025.
articles.body:
A new touring show about the Beatles' early years will be a lasting legacy of its writer, the late Stoke-on-Trent music promoter and record shop owner, Mike Lloyd.

The Rise of the Beatles is described as "a gig with narration" and tells the story of the Liverpool band's formation up until the moment they appeared at the King's Hall in Stoke in January 1963.

The gigs were Lloyd's final passion project, before his death in December, and came about after he was asked to do something for the city's centenary celebrations in 2025.

It was intended to be a one-off but is now being revived as a touring production.

Hundreds packed into King's Hall to see it as part of the centenary celebrations, and the new iteration opens at the Mitchell Arts Centre in Hanley on 23 November.

"We've decided that we want to carry on that legacy, because it's such a huge piece of the community that we don't want to let it go," said Lloyd's son Alex, speaking in January about the decision to stage the performances.

Opening at the Mitchell Arts Centre is particularly poignant, as Lloyd was a board member there.

Dave Shingler, friend and former employee, was asked by his family to put the Beatles show on and described it as partly storytelling and partly a tribute to the band.

"He really wanted to do a Beatles show that wasn't like any normal Beatles tribute act," Shingler said.

"He wanted to do something a little bit different – the idea of telling a story as well as putting the music on was at the forefront of it."

He added that he was not sure at first whether they would be able to do it due to all the various aspects of Lloyd's former business they were getting to grips with after his death.

He said he was "constantly second-guessing" whether Lloyd would have made the same decisions he was making but that he had been well supported by Lloyd's family and former colleagues.

"In the back of your head, you've always got, 'What would Mike have done? What would Mike think about this?'

"Every now and then it does hit you that he's not there; he's not coming through the door."

He said the Mitchell Arts Centre was "the best place to start the show" due to Lloyd being on the board there and his love for the venue.

The show continues to Bridgnorth and Telford after Hanley, with plans for other venues after that.

articles.title: US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
articles.summary: Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan is the current frontrunner, polls suggest, but the US and Russia could veto her bid.
articles.body:
A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.

With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.

Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.

The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.

“P5 member states are not as politically aligned as they have been in previous eras, arguably even during the Cold War,” said Holmes, referring to the permanent members of the UNSC.

The UN secretary-general has often been compared with a “secular pope” – a figure expected to unite countries and spearhead global diplomacy.

But the position is more than that of a figurehead. The secretary-general is also the UN’s top administrative official, responsible for tapping senior officials and supervising the UN Secretariat’s tens of thousands of staff.

“The secretary-general must be a skilled politician to navigate the geopolitics; a skilled diplomat and mediator to help settle disputes; a charismatic person in the public eye; and a solid and skilled administrator,” Jan Klabbers, professor of international law at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera. “It has been called ‘the most difficult job in the world’ for a reason.”

This year’s race comes as the UN, under Guterres, is under heavy strain, having been sidelined from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. It has faced blistering criticism from United States President Donald Trump and is suffering a financial crisis that has forced it to let go of thousands of staff.

It also comes as wider geopolitical rivalries extend to the pool of candidates to lead the organisation, who are being scrutinised over their nationalities and policy commitments.

Eight individuals who have been appointed by UN member states are currently in the running to replace Guterres. Most of them are from Latin America or the Caribbean, which is in line with representation according to informal UN protocol. Five of the eight are women, amid a push for the UN to select its first female secretary-general.

A leading contender, according to a series of anonymous straw polls the UNSC carries out to gauge support, is Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.

In the last poll on November 5, which does not show which UNSC members voted which way, Grynspan received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, according to PassBlue, a nonprofit that reports on UN affairs.

Grynspan, who heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been described as a “continuity candidate”, but there are concerns as to whether she would bring enough reform to an organisation facing huge political and financial pressures.

Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Grynspan had “solidified her position as the frontrunner”, but still appears to face opposition from the US and Russia, which could veto her bid.

While she has avoided directly confronting any veto-wielding nation, some of her reports as UNCTAD head have voiced concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, positions at odds with Washington’s more full-throated support for Israel. Grynspan has previously also disagreed with Russian justifications for suspending a deal to allow the transport of grain through the Black Sea.

At the same time, she — like other candidates — is believed to be lobbying with key member states to win their support. In April, she met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over her candidature.

“Grynspan’s team argue that they can still nudge Washington and Moscow to accept her, and US officials do seem to be leaving open the possibility of working with her in the end,” said Gowan.

To be elected, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour in the 15-member UNSC, while avoiding any vetoes from its five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGA) then ultimately has to sign off.

Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society campaign “advocating for a fair, open, inclusive way to select the next secretary-general”, stressed that opposition from P5 members in a straw poll does not necessarily equate to an eventual veto.

“It has been used in the past as a basis to extract a concession from a candidate, very often in the form of a backroom deal to get a P5 national appointed to a key role in the future UN boss’s cabinet,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Argentinian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, is also in the running. He finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes. However, his reputation for being closely aligned with Washington is expected to hurt him with some P5 members, especially China and Russia, though he has also had warm words for Beijing and Moscow in recent weeks.

The other candidates from Latin America or the Caribbean are Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett , Antigua and Barbuda diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.

Rodrigues Birkett, whose description of Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide” has drawn scrutiny in the US, received five “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll. Espinosa and A-Baki received 10 and 14 “discourage” votes, respectively, making their candidacies unlikely.

The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh and Turkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioglu, nominated by their countries in recent weeks, have also shaken up the race but face significant opposition.

Nusseibeh is reportedly favoured by the US and Russia, but her candidacy has received pushback over her country’s alleged arming of paramilitary forces accused of atrocities in Sudan. The United Arab Emirates has denied the allegation. Nusseibeh received six “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll.

“Nusseibeh’s main challenge is to win over China, which has so far seemed sceptical about her candidacy,” said Gowan. “If she can get Beijing’s support, she could break through.”

Sinirlioglu’s candidature, which UNSC member Greece is expected to oppose, received eight “discourage” votes.

Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu, the only remaining African candidate, received nine “discourage” votes.

Far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, though not an official candidate, has also been floated by the US as an outside choice, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

Several analysts told Al Jazeera that Grynspan appears to be in the best position, though the influence of P5 countries could change the race.

Earlier this month, the US and Russia put their weight behind the UAE’s Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.

China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.

Ellen Ravndal, associate professor in political science at the University of Stavanger, Norway, told Al Jazeera the drawn-out selection process and struggle to reach consensus reflect an era of “more geopolitical tensions” and a UN that is in “near-constant crisis mode”.

Adam Day, head of the Geneva office of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research, pointed out that while the leadership contest has been lengthier and more contested than in the previous cycles in which former Secretaries-General Guterres in 2016 and Ban Ki-moon in 2006 were elected, some earlier races stretched into December.

“In the broader scope of secretary-general races, this one is still within the range of what has been normal,” Day told Al Jazeera. “But the longer it takes, the less time the incoming secretary-general has to prepare a transition.”

If no successor to Guterres is selected by the end of the year, the UN Charter does not specify an automatic interim successor. Any gap in the post would therefore require the UNSC and other UN bodies to agree on how to manage organisational leadership and operations.

“There is widespread concern that the United States and possibly other influential states are running down the clock, potentially to increase pressure to settle for a less popular candidate or to leave the UN leaderless and weakened for a period,” said Donaldson.

articles.title: Officials say a tanker’s steering failed before it crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans
articles.summary: A tanker’s steering system failed and kept its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans, U.S. government safety officials said Sunday.
articles.body: A tanker’s steering system failed and kept its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans, U.S. government safety officials said Sunday. The preliminary finding from National Transportation Safety Board officials provided the first official word on what caused Friday’s crash of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker into the American Heritage cruise ship, which sent passengers, crew and two police officers plunging into the Mississippi River. NTSB officials said during a briefing in New Orleans that it’s not yet clear what caused the steering failure. “It could be many different things,” NTSB accident investigator Bart Barnum said. “That is something that we’re investigating very closely.” The tanker, measuring about 520 feet long, had a crew of 19. The cruise ship, about 300 feet long, had 140 passengers and 50 crew onboard. Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital, including the two police officers who were thrown into the river when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical. As of Sunday, six people remained hospitalized, the city of New Orleans said in a statement. The tanker’s steering problem caused its rudder to remain in a starboard position, to the right, which sent the tanker veering toward the east bank of the river, where it hit the cruise ship two minutes after the rudder became stuck, Barnum said. As the tanker approached the river’s east bank, the ship’s data recorder captured audio sounds “consistent” with the ship’s whistle going off, along with warnings and requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel’s marine radio, Barnum said. He added the data included commands to deploy the vessel anchors and emergency ship handling orders. NTSB Member John DeLeeuw urged people with photos or video of the crash to submit them to his agency to help with its investigation, which is expected to result in a preliminary report within 30 days. He also praised the “the excellent response” from federal, state, local and private vessels that helped rescue people immediately after the crash. The cruise ship capsized in 22 minutes, DeLeeuw said. Just hours after the crash, the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed a federal lawsuit saying that the tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

articles.title: Students must adapt to AI, says Guernsey education boss
articles.summary: A new survey is launched to learn how to best prepare students for future workplaces.
articles.body:
The head of an education provider has said students will need to adapt to changing employer demands due to new technology and artificial intelligence (AI).

The Guernsey Institute (TGI) has launched a survey asking employers what skills they expect employees to need in the future.

Executive principal Dr Louise Misselke said it was the first survey of its kind for 12 years and she foreshadowed AI would play a big part of the responses.

"People will need to change and adapt and upskill and retrain, but I actually think there's a lot of opportunity in those changes," she said.

Speaking about whether data should be gathered more frequently, Misselke said: "Ideally, of course, we'd like that to happen every year.

"We really need to hear those voices from employers about what qualifications and training they need to fill the skills gaps that they tell us they have."

Simon Le Tocq, chief executive of the institute's business school said "we need to do more to invest in our people".

He said: "The half-life of skills is decreasing, so in other words a skill which would maybe last for five years... it's a year-and-a-half.

"Our people are our competitive advantage in Guernsey, we can't compete on cost, we can't compete on size, so we have to compete on capability."

Esther Reid, dean at TGI University Centre, which offers education to over-18s, wanted the results of the survey to be used to keep workers in the island.

"We want people to know that even if they do go away for their initial higher education study, that they can move back to change their career or advance their professional learning," she said.

"It's really important that, from young people through to adult learners, we hear their voice in this."

articles.title: Jersey pupils fascinated by space get astronomy lesson
articles.summary: Pupils at First Tower School get a visit from a University of Cambridge astronomer.
articles.body:
Jersey primary school children have enjoyed learning about space in a lesson delivered by an astronomer.

Dr Robin Catchpole of the Cambridge Institute of Astronomy was invited to the island by the Jersey Astronomy Club and shared his extensive knowledge with pupils aged 10 and 11 at First Tower School.

Year 6 pupil Lola, 11, said her favourite part was learning about how the planets were created while Vihaan, 10, said he was fascinated by black holes and how they were formed.

Catchpole, who has written and co-written more than 100 research papers and articles on astronomy, said his trick for making space accessible to children was to show them planets they would be familiar with.

Catchpole said he first became interested in astronomy when his grandfather gave him a book about the subject and his mother showed him the Moon through a telescope on the beachfront in Torquay, Devon.

"I saw craters and shadows of mountains and I thought that was very exciting," he said.

Year 6 teacher Lee Bradshaw said it was a great opportunity to have an expert like Catchpole answering questions and children proved inquisitive about the subject.

articles.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
articles.summary: Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw gas field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty.
articles.body:
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.

Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.

It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.

The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences

Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.

"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.

"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."

Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.

"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."

Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".

She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".

Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.

This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.

He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".

A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.

The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.

The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.

Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.

But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully .

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined .

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.
